foundations.quizTarget: After editing the message, you run the previous executable without rebuilding. What can appear?

essentialSupport.fact: rustc translates a Rust source file into an executable. Editing main.rs does not change an already-built executable.
This course uses stable Rust 1.99.1 with edition 2024. An edition is not the same thing as a compiler version; one compiler can support several editions.
Cargo reads a manifest named Cargo.toml. The early single-file examples can also be compiled directly with rustc.
These fixtures need no downloaded crates or nightly features. The app shows concepts and checks rather than a Rust browser runner.

foundations.reasoning: Source edits and executable generation are separate steps.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace both operands with 5.0 and 2.0. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: u8 holds unsigned whole numbers from 0 through 255. i32 is a signed 32-bit type; usize is an unsigned size/index type whose width follows the target.
A suffix such as 3u8 selects a type explicitly. Without other constraints, an integer variable commonly defaults to i32.
f64 represents approximate fractions with finite precision. A numeric type is not a guarantee that every real-world quantity fits exactly.
5 /2 uses integer division. 5.0 /2.0 uses floating-point division; Rust does not implicitly mix an integer variable with a floating one.

foundations.reasoning: The changed operands make the division floating-point.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the added amount from 10 to 3. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Ordinary integer overflow can panic when overflow checks are enabled and can behave differently with other compilation settings. Do not use build settings as an implicit validation policy.

The dot in value.checked_add(10) selects a method on value; the parentheses supply the added amount. For u8, checked_add returns Some(result) if the sum fits and None if it does not. These are explicit success/absence variants; later lessons develop Option fully.
{:?} asks for a Debug representation. It displays Some(253) or None here, unlike an ordinary numeric display.
The example uses checked_add, so its behavior does not depend on whether ordinary overflow checks were enabled.

foundations.reasoning: The sum 253 is within 0 through 255, so the method reports a present result.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the value to 3.9. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: value as i32 converts a primitive numeric value to i32. It is not a text parser.
For this finite in-range float, conversion to i32 discards the fractional part toward zero rather than rounding to nearest.
Float-to-int casts have defined saturation and NaN rules, not a guarantee that the original measurement was suitable. Validate bounds and meaning separately.
Other conversion APIs can report failure where appropriate. Do not treat every as conversion as lossless.

foundations.reasoning: This in-range positive value truncates to 3.

foundations.quizTarget: Set denominator to 0. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Rust conditions require Boolean expressions; a nonzero integer is not automatically a true condition.
&& skips its right operand when the left is false. || skips its right operand when the left is true.
The denominator check comes before division. A zero denominator makes the left side false and prevents evaluation of the division.
Short-circuiting determines which operations run, not just the final Boolean.

foundations.reasoning: The guard fails and skips division by zero.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the text to "A". What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A single-quoted char such as 'é' is a Unicode scalar value, not merely one UTF-8 byte and not a complete grapheme cluster in every case.
String::from("é") creates an owned growable String. A double-quoted string literal provides an &str borrowed text view; full borrowing rules follow later.
String.len counts UTF-8 bytes. chars().count counts Unicode scalar values. Neither is a universal count of user-perceived characters.
The sample é uses two UTF-8 bytes and one scalar value. ASCII A uses one byte and one scalar value.

foundations.reasoning: The two counts coincide for ASCII but differ for the original sample.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the first tuple element to 5. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: (3,"read") is a tuple containing an integer and a text view. Tuple positions can have different types.
let (count,label)=item binds the first element to count and the second to label. Names do not select elements by spelling.
item.0 accesses the first tuple field. Tuple positions are fixed in its type.
The placeholders consume the supplied arguments in order.

foundations.reasoning: The declaration binds positions and the print controls presentation order.

foundations.quizTarget: Change only the assignment index to 2. What does the unchanged print show?

essentialSupport.fact: [2,4,6] is a three-element array. Its length is part of its type.
values[0] is the first element and values[2] the third. len gives the element count, not the last valid index.
let mut values allows assigning an array element. A normal immutable binding does not permit that mutation.
A runtime invalid index panics; it does not extend the array. Safe alternatives such as get return an Option.

foundations.reasoning: The changed assignment targets the third element.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the break value to 9. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: loop has no condition of its own. break exits it; continuing forever is not useful merely because it compiles.
break 7 sends 7 out of the loop expression. The surrounding let can store that result.
The body reaches break on its first pass, so no timing or overflow assumption is needed.
for visits a sequence and while repeats while a Boolean remains true. This lesson isolates the value-producing loop form.

foundations.reasoning: The first pass exits with the new value.

foundations.quizTarget: Add a semicolon after value*2 in the function body without adding return. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: fn double(value:i32)->i32 takes an i32 and promises an i32 result.
value*2 without a trailing semicolon is the block’s result expression.
Adding a semicolon turns that expression into a statement; the block would then return unit (), which does not match this i32 signature.
return value*2; exits with that value. This example uses the final-expression style.

foundations.reasoning: The trailing semicolon removes the expression result, producing unit rather than i32.

foundations.quizTarget: Move the text print after the closing brace. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: Ownership determines who is responsible for a value and when its resources are released. When an owner goes out of scope, its value is dropped unless ownership has moved.
A binding declared inside a block is not available outside that block.
An owned String controls heap-backed text as well as its local binding. The principle is about responsibility, not simply where bytes live.
This example prints the String inside its owning scope, then continues after the block.

foundations.reasoning: The binding is not available outside the block that declares it.

foundations.quizTarget: After moving source into target, print source instead. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: let target=source moves an owned String into target. The old binding cannot then be used as another owner of the same String.
Small scalar types such as i32 implement Copy. Assigning one copies its value and leaves the original usable.
The formatting macro can inspect target without taking its ownership in this example.
Assignment syntax looks similar for a String and an i32, but their types determine whether Copy applies.

foundations.reasoning: String does not implement Copy, so the ownership transfer makes the old binding unavailable for use.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the appended char to'?'. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: source.clone() asks the type to create another value. For String it duplicates the text storage so each String can own its contents.
Cloning does not move the source String into the destination.
push adds a char to the mutable cloned String. It does not change the original String’s separate storage.
Other types can define Clone differently, including sharing referenced resources. Read the type’s contract.

foundations.reasoning: The clone owns its separate String storage and receives the changed append.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the String content to "stars". What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: &text creates a shared reference to text. It allows reading while ownership stays with text.
The &String parameter receives a reference. Returning its length does not require taking the String away from the caller.
The borrowed call ends and the caller can still print text.
A reference must not outlive the data and cannot be used to mutate through shared access. Full aliasing restrictions follow next.

foundations.reasoning: The shared borrow permits inspection and leaves the owner valid.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the starting score to 7. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: &mut score creates a mutable reference. Through that reference, *value designates the original i32 for assignment. *value += 1 adds one and stores the result back through that reference.
let mut score makes the original binding mutable so it may be mutably borrowed.
You cannot keep simultaneously usable conflicting shared and mutable borrows of the same data. The rule prevents unsynchronized conflicting access in safe Rust.
A function without an explicit return type returns unit (). It performs its update through the borrowed reference.

foundations.reasoning: The dereferenced mutable reference selects the caller’s original score.

foundations.quizTarget: Move text.push before the print of view. What happens?

essentialSupport.fact: The compiler can determine that a shared borrow is no longer used after its final access. Its effective restriction need not last to the closing brace.
Here view is printed before text.push, so the shared borrow is no longer needed when mutation begins.
If text.push occurs before a later print of view, the mutable access overlaps a still-needed shared borrow and is rejected.
No runtime borrow counter is used for these ordinary references. Later RefCell has a different runtime-checked mechanism.

foundations.reasoning: The later read keeps the shared borrow needed across the attempted mutation.

foundations.quizTarget: Remove the push call. What length prints?

essentialSupport.fact: vec![2,4] constructs a vector of elements. Unlike a fixed array, its length can change.
let mut values permits push to append an element. len returns the current number of elements.
A vector may reserve more storage than currently initialized elements. Only valid indices below len can be read.
Rust prevents growing a vector while an incompatible live reference to one of its elements is still being used.

foundations.reasoning: The constructor already supplies two elements; the removed call would have added a third.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the borrowed range to 0..2. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: The slice type [T] describes a contiguous sequence; &[T] is a borrowed reference to it. &values[1..3] borrows elements at indices 1 and 2, excluding 3, without owning a copied collection.
view[0] refers to the original values[1], because the view starts one position into the array.
The slice reference remains tied to the underlying array’s valid lifetime.
The start and end must describe a valid range. An invalid checked range panics rather than creating arbitrary storage.

foundations.reasoning: The new start changes the first element while the half-open length remains two.

foundations.quizTarget: Change the initializer to None. What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Option<T> is either Some(value) or None. The type parameter T names the kind of value that may be present.
match examines the variant. Each arm uses pattern => result, and commas separate arms. Some(value) binds the payload; None selects the absence branch.
This program deliberately maps absence to 0. Other tasks may need to report missing data instead.
unwrap would panic on None. Matching lets the program handle absence without assuming it away.

foundations.reasoning: The None arm defines the fallback result.

foundations.quizTarget: Replace Ok(7) with Err(String::from("missing")). What prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Result<T,E> contains Ok(value) or Err(error). T and E are the success and error types.
match binds the successful value or error payload. This example uses a String as the error message.
Constructing Err does not unwind the program. The surrounding code chooses how to handle or propagate it.
Real operations often provide structured error types. A String here keeps the initial success/failure distinction visible.

foundations.reasoning: Err is handled by the authored failure branch instead of causing automatic unwinding.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the input becomes "many", what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: On a Result, ? extracts the Ok value or returns early with the Err, converting its error type if needed. The enclosing function must have a compatible return type; ? is not a panic or an instruction to ignore errors.

text.parse::<u32>() requests an unsigned32-bit integer. The ::<...> syntax supplies a type argument explicitly. ParseIntError is the parser’s error type. use std::num::ParseIntError brings that standard-library name into this scope; it does not download a dependency. Here both layers use that same type, so failure propagates directly.

types-and-design.reasoning: The parse error returns from minutes immediately and main selects its Err branch.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the print tries session.topic instead of topic after the move, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A struct groups named fields. A field of type String owns its string data; assigning that field to another binding moves it unless it is explicitly borrowed or cloned.

After moving one non-Copy field, that field cannot be used through the original value. Other independent Copy fields can still be used when the type has no custom Drop implementation. Do not describe every struct assignment as a deep copy.

types-and-design.reasoning: Moving session.topic transfers ownership; the original field is no longer available to read.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If mut is removed from the counter binding, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: Methods are defined in impl Type. &self borrows shared access, &mut self borrows exclusive mutable access, and self takes ownership of the receiver unless its type is Copy. Method-call syntax handles ordinary borrowing automatically.
The inc method changes n through &mut self. The caller must permit a mutable borrow of its Counter. read uses &self and does not consume it. The small counts avoid arithmetic overflow.

types-and-design.reasoning: The method requires exclusive mutable access, but the binding no longer allows that borrow.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If label receives State::Waiting, what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: An enum names alternatives, and each alternative may carry a payload. State::Ready(String) contains text while State::Waiting contains none. Construct a variant with its path; it is not a separate unrelated type.

match chooses a branch and can return a value. Matching Ready(text) binds its owned String payload here. A match over the enum must cover all possible cases; a missing variant cannot simply be ignored.

types-and-design.reasoning: The no-payload Waiting alternative has its own branch returning waiting.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the input becomes Some(0), what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A match guard adds if condition after a pattern. Some(n) if n > 0 handles only present positive values; the following Some(_) still handles other present values. _ ignores a matched value.

Match selects the first matching arm whose guard succeeds. A guard is not a replacement for covering remaining cases. This classification keeps None distinct from a present zero. The returned string literals have type &'static str: their text is available for the entire program, not allocated inside the function.

types-and-design.reasoning: The Some pattern matches but its positive guard fails, so the later Some arm handles the value.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If Topic stores "Maps", what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: A trait specifies behavior a type can implement. impl Label for Topic supplies the method required by Label. The &self receiver borrows the object rather than consuming it. struct Topic(String) declares a tuple struct with one unnamed String field; Topic(...) constructs it and .0 selects that field.

The trait method returns a borrowed string slice tied to the borrow of self by lifetime elision. &self.0 borrows the first field of this tuple struct; String can be viewed as &str. This is not class inheritance.

types-and-design.reasoning: The implementation returns a slice of this Topic’s stored String, so its contents determine the output.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If b.x becomes 3, what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: #[derive(...)] requests generated implementations when every field supports the necessary behavior. Debug supports {:?} formatting; PartialEq supports ==. Deriving does not bypass a field’s trait requirements.

Clone explicitly duplicates a value according to its implementation. Copy permits implicit bitwise value copying and requires Clone; it cannot be derived for a struct containing String. An all-u32 record can derive both, but owning String data needs ownership-aware treatment.

types-and-design.reasoning: The generated PartialEq compares the corresponding x values, which are now different.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If second becomes String::from("three"), what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A type parameter in Pair<T> lets the fields share a type chosen by each use. T is not an untyped box; the compiler still checks each concrete instantiation.
Pair { first: 2, second: 3 } can infer one integer type for both fields. Mixing a String with a u32 cannot satisfy one T. If the fields need unrelated types, declare two type parameters deliberately.

types-and-design.reasoning: The first field fixes T to u32, but the changed second field supplies String.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the impl Label for Topic block is removed, can the two calls still compile?

essentialSupport.fact: T: Label constrains a generic type to implement Label. A generic function can call label because the bound promises it. Rust normally monomorphizes such generic uses into concrete code; the bound is not a runtime search for a missing method. struct Topic; is a unit-like struct with no fields; the expression Topic creates its value without constructor parentheses.

&dyn Label is a borrowed trait object using runtime method dispatch. The trait must support dynamic use; not every trait does. Here the same contract supports a generic borrowed call and a dynamic borrowed call without transferring ownership.

types-and-design.reasoning: The generic bound and conversion to the trait object both require Topic to implement Label; neither dispatch mechanism removes that contract.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If use_left is false, what prints while both strings remain alive?

essentialSupport.fact: A lifetime parameter such as 'a relates borrowed inputs to a borrowed output. It does not extend any object’s life or choose how long memory physically exists.

Both arguments and the returned slice use 'a below because either input may be returned. The caller must keep whichever reference the contract permits valid for the result’s use. Annotations describe the guarantee; they do not make a local String live forever.

types-and-design.reasoning: The Boolean selects the second borrowed input; the lifetime annotation expresses validity rather than which branch executes.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If view creates a local String and returns &local instead, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: Returning &str borrowed from an input can be valid because the caller owns the underlying String. With one input reference, lifetime elision relates that input to the returned reference.

A String created inside a function is dropped when that function returns unless ownership leaves the function. Returning a slice into that local would dangle, so safe Rust rejects it. Adding a lifetime label cannot repair the owner’s early destruction; return an owned String instead when appropriate.

types-and-design.reasoning: The local String would be destroyed before the caller could use its slice; returning ownership would be a different valid design.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the first next() call is removed, what does the remaining call print?

essentialSupport.fact: An iterator produces items through next. map transforms items lazily: constructing it does not eagerly build a vector. A closure uses |argument| expression syntax; here it doubles each integer when requested.

into_iter on the vector takes ownership of its elements. next needs a mutable iterator binding and returns Option: Some(item) when available, None when exhausted. Each call advances; it does not restart the source.

types-and-design.reasoning: Without the first consumption, the iterator still points at its first mapped item.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If a println!("{count}") is inserted between the two increment calls, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: A closure can borrow captured variables. || denotes a closure with no explicit parameters. A closure that increments count needs a mutable borrow of count and a mutable closure binding when called.

While the closure will still be used, the captured mutable borrow prevents conflicting reads or writes of count. After its last use, non-lexical lifetime analysis can let the outer code access count again. This is not a separate copied counter.

types-and-design.reasoning: The later closure call keeps its mutable capture live across the inserted shared read.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If main prints text after constructing length and before calling it, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: move makes a closure capture values by value. Capturing a String transfers ownership into the closure, so the original binding can no longer use it. Capturing a Copy value instead copies it.

A move closure is not automatically callable only once. This closure merely borrows its owned String to read len, so it can be called repeatedly. A closure that moves its captured String out would instead consume that capture when called.

types-and-design.reasoning: move transferred the String at closure creation even though each later call only borrows the captured value.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the second string becomes "bad", what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: collect consumes an iterator into a destination determined by a type annotation or explicit type argument. Iterating Result<T,E> items can collect into Result<Vec<T>,E>, rather than merely a vector of Results. The _ in the destination error-type position asks the compiler to infer that type from the parser.

Collecting into Result succeeds only when every item succeeds; the first Err ends collection and becomes the result. This does not invent a default value for bad input or promise that later items were processed.

types-and-design.reasoning: The destination is one Result wrapping the vector, so a parse failure makes the entire collection an Err.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the range changes to 0..1, what prints on the second line?

essentialSupport.fact: String and str are UTF-8 text. len reports bytes, while chars iterates Unicode scalar values. A scalar value is not always a whole user-perceived character; grapheme segmentation needs additional rules.

str.get(range) returns Option<&str> and rejects out-of-range indices or non-character-boundary byte positions. Direct indexing with an invalid range can panic. In "éa", é occupies two bytes, so 0..2 selects it but 0..1 splits its encoding.

types-and-design.reasoning: The ending byte offset is inside the two-byte UTF-8 encoding, so the checked get returns None.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the second word becomes "write", what is the read count?

essentialSupport.fact: HashMap<String, u32> owns its String keys. insert moves an owned key into the map; borrowing a key for lookup is a different operation. Hash-map iteration order is not a stable presentation order.

entry(key).or_insert(0) obtains mutable access to the existing value or inserts zero first. *count dereferences that mutable reference so += 1 updates the stored number. Repeating the same key updates one entry rather than making duplicates. get returns Option<&u32>; copied turns a present borrowed integer into its Copy value, and unwrap_or(0) supplies zero only when the Option is None.

types-and-design.reasoning: Only the first iteration now updates the read entry; the other creates a separate write entry.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the second insertion is "Go", what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: HashSet stores distinct values according to equality and hashing. insert reports true for a newly added value and false when an equal value was already present. It does not preserve insertion order for iteration.

len counts unique stored values; contains tests membership without removing anything. This example prints scalar facts instead of asserting a random hash iteration order. String slices here refer to static literal text.

types-and-design.reasoning: The second distinct value increases cardinality, while Rust remains a member.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If pub is removed from label, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: mod creates a module. Public visibility is opt-in with pub; a private function inside a child module is not accessible from its parent. A path such as helper::label names an item through its module.
use brings a name into scope; it does not fetch a dependency. crate:: starts at the current crate root. This inline-module example needs only one main.rs file and the standard library.

types-and-design.reasoning: A path does not bypass visibility; the parent cannot import the private child-module item.

types-and-design.quizTarget: If the local library returns n * 3, what prints after rebuilding?

essentialSupport.fact: A Cargo package has a manifest and one or more targets such as a binary or library crate. Edition selects language rules; it is not the compiler version. This fixture explicitly chooses edition2024 and only a local library dependency.

Save the files below, put the complete main example in src/main.rs, then run cargo run --offline --quiet from the package directory. path points to supplied local source rather than a registry. Offline does not conjure missing dependencies: all required sources must already be present.
```toml
# Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "lesson_app"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
[dependencies]
lesson_math = { path = "localmath" }
```
```toml
# localmath/Cargo.toml
[package]
name = "lesson_math"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
```
```rust
// localmath/src/lib.rs
pub fn double(n: u32) -> u32 { n * 2 }
```

types-and-design.reasoning: Cargo builds the supplied changed local dependency; the same call now returns three times six.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the unit test expects 1 for clamp(-1), what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: The clamp method caps n to the inclusive endpoints zero and ten. Save the main snippet as src/lib.rs. #[cfg(test)] includes the tests module only for test builds; #[test] registers a test function. use super::clamp brings the parent module’s function into scope. assert_eq! compares actual and expected values and reports a failing assertion.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The changed expectation is wrong; cargo test reports failure rather than modifying the function.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the input is "0", which result is displayed?

essentialSupport.fact: InvalidMinutes is a custom error type. Deriving Debug supports diagnostic formatting; implementing Display supplies the user-facing message. The fmt method borrows a Formatter destination; its underscore lifetime placeholder is inferred. fmt::Result is the formatting Result type, and write! returns that Result. Implementing std::error::Error marks it as a standard error type. It does not automatically add recovery or validation.

parse::<u8> may fail for nonnumeric text or values outside u8. map_err converts that error into InvalidMinutes; ? propagates it from parse_minutes. The range 1..=60 includes both endpoints. A separate range check rejects otherwise parsed values outside 1 through 60. This intentionally loses the original parse cause; richer errors could preserve it when useful.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Zero parses as u8 but fails the explicit domain range and becomes the custom error.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the second stored value changes from 4 to 9, what is the sum?

essentialSupport.fact: A recursive enum cannot contain another full copy of itself directly with no indirection. Box<List> stores an owning pointer to a heap-allocated List, giving the enum a finite representation. Dropping the box releases its owned allocation and nested values.

The tiny list owns a tail through Box. Matching &self borrows each node; n and tail are borrowed values, and the sum method reads them without taking ownership. The example uses two nodes only: recursive processing and recursive destruction are not a promise of unlimited stack capacity.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The borrowed traversal adds the head three to the changed tail nine.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If second is instead a new independent Rc allocation, what counts does first report?

essentialSupport.fact: Rc<T> is a reference-counted pointer for shared ownership within one thread. Rc::clone adds another strong owner of the same allocation. It does not clone the String itself. Rc::strong_count reports the current strong owner count in this controlled example.

drop(second) consumes and drops that owner now rather than waiting for its enclosing scope to end. The allocation remains while a strong owner exists. Rc uses non-atomic reference counts and is not Send or Sync; do not use it to share ownership across threads. Strong reference cycles can prevent reclamation; Weak is a separate tool for breaking those cycles.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: An independent Rc does not add an owner of first’s allocation, even when its String has equal contents.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the shared guard is dropped before try_borrow_mut, what is printed?

essentialSupport.fact: RefCell permits interior mutability through a shared reference, while enforcing the usual one-mutable-or-many-shared borrow rule at runtime. borrow and borrow_mut panic if the rule is violated; try_borrow_mut instead returns a Result so a conflict can be handled without a panic.

The value returned by borrow is a guard. While read remains alive, a mutable borrow cannot be granted. Explicitly dropping it ends that shared borrow, allowing the later mutable guard to change the value. RefCell is not a thread synchronization primitive.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: With no live shared guard, the temporary mutable borrow succeeds; the later update still stores nine.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If other is a separate Arc::new(7) rather than a clone, what is printed?

essentialSupport.fact: Arc<T> uses atomic reference counting for shared ownership. Arc can be sent and shared only when its inner type satisfies the required Send and Sync bounds. Arc alone does not make arbitrary inner mutation thread-safe; a Mutex or atomic payload may still be necessary.

Arc::get_mut returns an optional mutable reference only when there are no other Arc or Weak pointers to that allocation. With two strong owners it returns None. After dropping the other owner, this example has unique ownership and receives Some. No threads are started yet; the next lessons separate mutation and thread lifetime.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The independent allocation adds no owner of value, so value remains uniquely owned at both observations.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the protected addition changes from 4 to 9, what prints after the first guard is dropped?

essentialSupport.fact: Mutex::lock returns a Result containing a guard. Dereferencing the guard accesses the protected value. Dropping the guard releases the lock. Here expect makes the example stop with context if the mutex is poisoned, typically after a thread panicked while holding it; production recovery is a deliberate policy, not something to ignore.

The inner block bounds the first guard’s lifetime. The later lock occurs only after that guard was dropped, avoiding a recursive-lock assumption. This first example is single-threaded to isolate guard ownership; concurrent updates must all use the same mutex.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The guard mutates the protected integer and releases the lock at block exit; the later guard observes twelve.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the moved String is "explore", what result does join obtain?

essentialSupport.fact: thread::spawn starts a new operating-system thread. The move closure takes ownership of its captured String, so the worker does not borrow a local that might disappear. The final closure expression returns the String length.

JoinHandle::join waits and returns a Result containing the worker result or a panic payload. expect here makes a worker panic explicit rather than silently ignoring it. Dropping the handle would detach the worker, not wait for it. The sample makes no execution-order or speed promise.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The worker owns the changed String and returns its seven-byte length before join completes.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the sent String becomes "finished", what is received before the loop ends?

essentialSupport.fact: mpsc::channel creates a multi-producer, single-consumer channel with a Sender and Receiver. send moves this String into the channel; the sending code cannot keep using that moved String. Here only one worker sends, then its sender is dropped when the closure returns.

The for loop receives messages until all senders have been dropped and queued messages drained. Keeping an unused sender alive would keep the loop waiting. After collection, join still explicitly observes the worker’s completion and any panic.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The owned finished String is delivered; dropping the last sender ends iteration only after the queue is drained.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If this example uses Rc instead of Arc, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: Send means a value’s ownership may be transferred between threads; Sync means sharing &T between threads is safe. These are marker traits, usually derived automatically from a type’s contents. Do not write unsafe implementations merely to suppress a compiler error.

The worked value is Arc<i32>, which satisfies the relevant bounds. Replacing Arc with Rc asks thread::spawn to capture a non-Send reference-counted pointer; the compiler rejects that boundary before any thread executes. The correct repair depends on ownership and access needs, not just silencing a diagnostic.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Rc itself lacks Send; a safe inner integer does not repair its non-atomic shared ownership mechanism.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If each atomic update adds 2 instead of 1, what prints after both joins?

essentialSupport.fact: AtomicUsize::fetch_add performs an atomic addition and returns the previous value, which this example ignores. Arc lets the two workers own handles to the same counter. Each worker performs a bounded one hundred increments.

Ordering::SeqCst requests sequentially consistent ordering. It does not make several unrelated operations a single transaction or guarantee performance. Joining both workers bounds lifetime before the final load; no racy ordinary-counter variant or relaxed-ordering experiment is run.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Two workers perform one hundred additions of two each; atomic updates avoid lost increments.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the file is inside a nonexistent parent directory in this fixture, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: std::fs::write and read_to_string return Results. io::Result<T> aliases Result<T, io::Error>. The ? operator returns an error immediately from the helper when an operation fails. The caller decides how to report it. read_to_string also requires valid UTF-8, not merely a readable file.

Run only in a disposable working directory: this example creates or replaces notes.txt. These convenience functions manage their file handles, but successful writing is not a promise of durable storage after a power failure. Dropping a File does not provide a returned close error; durability and explicit synchronization require a separate policy.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: fs::write cannot create the missing parent directory; ? returns that error before reading.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If a third valid line is appended, what does this bounded parser report?

essentialSupport.fact: BufRead::lines yields Result<String> values with line endings removed. Use ? for each line read, not just when creating the reader. enumerate pairs each item with its zero-based index. Cursor makes this example read a fixed in-memory byte sequence, with no file or network access.

The helper checks the entire supplied input is at most thirty-two bytes before constructing the reader, then accepts at most two lines and minute values 1 through 60. Thus the sum is at most 120. On an unbounded external stream, checking a String length after lines allocated it would be too late; this lesson’s fixed input cap is part of its contract.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Enumeration reaches index two for the third line, triggering the explicit line-count rejection.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the joined final name becomes tomorrow.txt, what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: Path borrows a path and PathBuf owns one. join constructs a new path value; it does not create a directory or file. The representation and separator conventions depend on the target platform.

file_name returns an Option because some paths have no final filename. These literal relative paths do. Converting that OsStr with to_str is also optional because operating-system paths need not be valid UTF-8. Option::and_then calls its closure only for Some and flattens the returned Option rather than nesting it. The sample handles that possibility with a fallback instead of assuming every path is a String.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: join and file_name manipulate path values, not filesystem contents.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: With no user argument, what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: std::env::args yields Unicode command-line argument Strings. skip(1) omits the conventional program-name entry, then collect::<Vec<String>> stores the user arguments. If non-Unicode arguments must be supported, use args_os instead; args can panic on invalid Unicode.

Run this example as ./app read for the worked output. A slice pattern [topic] matches exactly one argument, borrowing that String. The fallback handles zero or several user arguments without indexing a missing item. This is an application policy, not shell parsing implemented by Rust.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The empty argument slice does not match [topic], so the fallback handles it without indexing.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the input changes to "61", what is returned to the display branch?

essentialSupport.fact: parse::<u32> checks whether text is a representable unsigned integer. It does not know whether a study session should permit zero or a very large duration. trim deliberately accepts leading and trailing whitespace; that normalization is part of the chosen policy.

The helper returns a descriptive Result after enforcing 1 through 60. This sample uses static string error messages, so no owned error allocation is needed. The success branch receives only a validated minute count; parse failure and range failure remain distinguishable.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Sixty-one parses successfully but violates the explicit application range.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If minutes becomes 20, what does the same Display implementation produce?

essentialSupport.fact: Implementing fmt::Display lets {} format a type. The fmt method borrows self and a mutable Formatter, then returns fmt::Result. The placeholder lifetime '_ means the compiler infers the borrow lifetime; it is not a new stored lifetime parameter on Session.

write!(f, ...) sends output to the caller’s formatter and returns any formatting error. The trailing expression returns that Result directly. Debug and Display serve different purposes; deriving Debug does not create this Display representation.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The implementation reads the current field and writes it followed by the chosen unit label.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If drop(future) is replaced by future.await in this ordinary main, what happens?

essentialSupport.fact: An async block produces a Future value describing work. Its body progresses only when the future is polled. Creating the future does not spawn a thread, start a timer or install an executor. This example deliberately drops an unpolled future.

The .await syntax is allowed inside an async function or block, not this ordinary main. An executor is responsible for polling and wakeups for general asynchronous work. No Tokio or other runtime is used here; the next lesson polls only an already-ready standard-library future once, not arbitrary I/O.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: A future remains lazy, and .await has a language context requirement; a normal main cannot use it directly.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If ready is constructed with 11, what does the one poll produce?

essentialSupport.fact: Future::poll takes a pinned mutable receiver and a task Context, returning Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending. Box::pin constructs a pinned heap value; as_mut reborrows it as Pin<&mut _>. Pin supports address-stability contracts for types that require them, not a blanket ban on moving every Rust value.

future::ready returns a future guaranteed to produce Ready on its poll. Waker::noop ignores wake requests, so it cannot drive general futures that become ready later. Context::from_waker supplies that waker for this single bounded poll. Never turn this into a spin loop or poll the completed future again; this is not a general executor.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: The ready constructor already owns its final output, so one poll returns the changed value immediately.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the expansion becomes ($value) + ($value), what prints?

essentialSupport.fact: macro_rules! defines syntax patterns. In ($value:expr), $value captures one expression; the expansion uses it in ordinary Rust code. The ! at a call site distinguishes macro invocation from a normal function call.

This twice macro binds the captured expression once to a local value, then uses that value twice. The input block increments calls and returns three. Duplicating $value in two evaluated positions instead would evaluate the input twice; a macro does not automatically guarantee single evaluation.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Each expanded occurrence executes the block, incrementing calls once; both returned threes still add to six.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the requested index is 1, what does the safe access produce?

essentialSupport.fact: Unsafe operations have conditions the programmer must uphold when the compiler cannot verify them. An unsafe block does not disable borrowing rules everywhere, make invalid memory valid or turn undefined behavior into a predictable demonstration. Safe public wrappers must enforce their own invariants before relying on unsafe internals.

slice.get returns an Option after checking the index, so this example needs no unsafe block at all. By contrast, get_unchecked requires a valid in-bounds index even if its result is not later used. We do not call it with an invalid index or execute any undefined-behavior example.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Index one is within the two-element slice, so get returns a valid borrowed element.

library-and-concurrency.quizTarget: If the first text changes to "70", what is collected and summed?

essentialSupport.fact: This fixed array contains four text inputs. parse::<u32>().ok() converts a parse Result to an Option, and filter_map keeps only Some values. The range filter then keeps minute counts from 1 through 60. This intentionally skips invalid inputs rather than misrepresenting them as valid zero-minute sessions.

take(2) keeps at most two accepted values. collect builds a Vec<u32>, and iter().sum::<u32>() totals its borrowed elements. Since each retained value is at most sixty, the total is bounded by 120. This is an in-memory teaching pipeline, not durable storage or a complete error-reporting application.

library-and-concurrency.reasoning: Seventy parses but fails the range rule; bad fails parsing and zero fails the range, leaving only twenty.
